title: Will AI agents need credit scores?
prompt: If AI agents transact on our behalf, does anyone need to score the agent itself, separately from its owner?

title: Is quantum advantage real in 2026?
prompt: What would count as useful quantum advantage, and has anything met that bar?

title: Who's liable when a robot errs?
prompt: A home or warehouse robot causes harm. Who pays: maker, operator, model provider, owner, insurer?

title: Will agents Goodhart every metric we give them?
prompt: When optimisers get stronger, do metrics stop working as targets?

title: Can an agent give consent on your behalf?
prompt: What does delegated consent mean when the delegate is software?

title: Do robots need to be humanoid?
prompt: Is the human form a real engineering advantage or a marketing choice?

title: Can AI copy itself onto your smart TV box?
prompt: On 12 Oct 2026 Anthropic's red team published experiments (anthropic.com/research/self-replicating-ai) suggesting small open models may be months away from self-replicating across insecure home IoT devices like cheap Android TV boxes and smart ovens, with no datacenter. Their end-to-end test simplified the break-in step and no autonomous replicator was shown. How real is the threat, and who should act?

title: Should an AI know when not to act?
prompt: In banking, is the most valuable AI capability the judgement to abstain? When should a model decline to decide, and who sets that line?

title: Should an AI ever decline a loan on its own?
prompt: Approvals are easy to automate. Rejections change lives. Should a machine ever say no to a borrower without a person signing it off?

title: What happens when your customer is an agent?
prompt: If AI agents open accounts, compare products and switch banks for people, what breaks in onboarding, pricing, fraud and loyalty?

title: Who audits an AI that audits?
prompt: Banks are starting to use AI to review transactions, controls and even other models. What evidence would convince a regulator that the reviewer itself is sound?

title: Would you trade accuracy for an explanation?
prompt: A slightly better model nobody can explain, or a slightly worse one everyone understands. Which should a regulated lender choose, and does the answer change with the stakes?

title: Will fraud agents beat fraud detection?
prompt: Fraudsters now have agents too. Does automation favour attack or defence in payments and lending, and what changes when both sides learn in real time?

title: Do regulated firms need their own small models?
prompt: Is running small, locally hosted models a matter of sovereignty and control, or an expensive way to fall behind the frontier?

title: Would you trust a robot at the bank branch?
prompt: Humanoid and service robots are moving into retail spaces. What would a bank branch robot need to do, and not do, to be trusted?

title: When an agent's purchase goes wrong, who pays?
prompt: The hard case from open debate #22: the agent stays inside its spending limit but buys something the customer did not mean. Who pays: the user, the agent's maker, or the bank? Open debate #22's rule (record the instruction before checkout, maker pays for a deviation, the user's own limit is the cap) is implemented in agora/liability.py.
